tip: 'Dont' replaces 'de + qui/quoi': 'le collègue dont je t'ai parlé' = whom I told you about ('parler de').
No 'a' before a profession after 'être': 'je serais médecin' = I'd be a doctor. You normally add 'un' only when you describe it – 'un bon médecin'.
After 'que', the participle quietly agrees with the noun before it: 'reçu' stays bare for masculine 'le cadeau', but a feminine noun would force 'reçue'.
'Il faudra' has no real subject – 'il' is a dummy placeholder: 'il faudra se remettre au travail' = 'one will have to' get back to work. It comes from 'falloir'.
'S'occuper' always needs 'de' for what you handle: 'qui s'occupe de mon père' = who takes care of my father. Drop the 'de' and the sentence breaks.
'Assister à' means to attend, not to assist – a false friend: 'assister à la réunion' = to be at the meeting. To help someone is 'aider'.
For an action finished before another future one, French uses the future perfect: 'aurons vendu' = will have sold. English just says 'have sold'.
French uses the present with 'depuis' for something still going on: 'attend depuis une heure' = has been waiting for an hour, and still is.
The 'si' half never takes the conditional – the setup stays in the imperfect: 'même si j'avais... je ne l'achèterais pas' = even if I had... I wouldn't buy it.
'Tu verras' = 'you'll see' is everyday reassurance, not a literal claim about eyesight: 'tu verras, tout ira bien'. Same use as 'on verra' = we'll see.
After 'si', French keeps the present even for a future 'if': 'si tu étudies... tu réussiras'. But 'quand' and 'dès que' DO take the future.
'Arriver' builds its past with 'être', not 'avoir': the would-have form is 'serait arrivée', never 'aurait arrivé'.
English 'should have' becomes 'aurions dû', literally 'would have had to'. Past regret = conditional of 'devoir' + infinitive.
'Il aurait fallu' = 'we should have', but names nobody: 'falloir' only ever runs with a dummy 'il' – 'il aurait fallu réserver'.
'Nul ne' is a bookish 'no one', working like 'personne ne': 'nul ne croyait' = 'no one believed'. The 'ne' stays and there's no 'pas' with these negatives.
'Sans que' forces the subjunctive: 'sans qu'elle le sût' = without her knowing. Trigger words like 'sans que' and 'avant que' always pull this mood.
English says 'when you finish', but here French puts the future after 'quand': 'quand tu auras fini' = once you'll have finished.
French uses 'où' (literally 'where') for time too: 'le jour où' = 'the day when', never 'the day where'. Same with 'l'année où' and 'le moment où'.
English can drop the 'that' – 'the song you're singing' – but French can never drop 'que': 'la chanson que tu chantes'.
'Venir de' + verb means 'just did', not 'come to': 'viennent d'emménager' = 'just moved in'. A present-tense verb covers the recent past.
'En' + the '-ant' form means 'while/on doing': 'en partant' = 'as I was leaving'. French mostly saves this '-ant' shape for the 'en' combo.
After 'quand', French uses the future where English uses the present perfect: 'nous aurons déjeuné' = 'when we've had lunch'. No present tense here.
Color words land after the noun in French: 'un chapeau rouge', not 'un rouge chapeau'. Most everyday adjectives follow the noun this way.
After 'avant de', French wants the infinitive, not the -ing form: 'avant de déménager' = 'before moving'. Same pattern with 'sans' and 'pour' + infinitive.
'Manquer' flips the subject: 'lui manque' means the country is missing TO him, so HE misses it. The thing missed is the subject; the person is 'lui', 'me', 'te'.
The 'si' half never takes the conditional: 'si tu avais fait' (had done), then 'tu aurais compris' (would have understood). Only the result half gets 'would'.
Two past tenses split the job: 'me préparais' (imperfect) sets the ongoing scene, 'tu m'as envoyé' (perfect) is the single action that cuts in.
'Quoique' (one word) = 'although'; 'quoi que' (two words) = 'whatever'. Here 'quoiqu'elle eût' means 'although she had', and the verb turns subjunctive.
'Prise' agrees with 'la décision' (feminine singular): 'pris' → 'prise'.
'Dont' replaces possessive 'de': 'le titre du film' → 'dont j'ai oublié le titre'.
